note.text: A partnership brings co-owners together to conduct a business and share its outcomes under an agreement. Partners may combine funds, skills and work, but must coordinate decisions. A partnership agreement can specify contributions, duties, profit sharing and handling disputes or departures. This introductory comparison uses an ordinary general partnership; limited-partnership forms differ. In that ordinary model, personal liability may be extensive. Do not assume that profit is shared equally or only according to capital unless the agreement says so.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain shared ownership and calculate a partner’s agreed profit share. Builds on: the sole proprietor’s finance and control limits. Leads to: companies and the distinction between owners’ liability and business debts.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: Bih supplies equipment and Ayuk provides funds to an imaginary Bamenda workshop. They agree on duties and a profit-sharing ratio. A disagreement about opening hours reveals a coordination cost. Their classroom agreement is an economic illustration, not a legally sufficient document or advice about the correct OHADA form.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Read the agreement in the question. Separate capital contributions from profit allocations. Add ratio parts before dividing the distributable total, and check the partners’ shares sum to that total. Explain both the benefit of pooled resources and the possibility of conflict.

solution: Bih receives {a}/{a+b} of {total}, giving {answer} CFA francs.
